title: Medium exam 4
about: Ten single-choice questions that combine two facts or ask you to trace two or three steps: what root can and cannot do, depth limits, string and file tests, whole words and substitutions.

questions.title: Root and permissions
questions.text: `f` has mode `---------` and `s.sh` is a correct script with mode `rw-r--r--`; both belong to ana. Root runs `cat f` and then `./s.sh`. What happens?

options.t: Both fail with `Permission denied`, because root is also subject to the permission bits.
options.why: Root can read and write any file regardless of its bits.

options.t: Both work, because root has every permission on every file.
options.why: Root can read any file, but to execute a file at least one `x` bit has to be set.

options.t: `cat f` prints the content, but `./s.sh` fails with `Permission denied`.
options.why: Root needs no read permission, yet still needs an `x` bit somewhere to run a file.

options.t: `cat f` fails, but `./s.sh` works, because it has read permission.
options.why: The opposite: root ignores the read and write bits but not the missing execute bit.

questions.title: Limiting the depth
questions.text: `d` contains `a.txt`, `s/b.txt` and `s/t/c.txt`. What does `find d -maxdepth 2 -name '*.txt'` print?

options.t: `d/a.txt` only
options.why: `d/a.txt` is at depth 1, but `d/s/b.txt` at depth 2 is also within the limit.

options.t: `d/a.txt` and `d/s/b.txt`
options.why: `d` is depth 0, its entries depth 1 and the entries of `d/s` depth 2; `c.txt` is at depth 3.

options.t: `d/a.txt`, `d/s/b.txt` and `d/s/t/c.txt`
options.why: `c.txt` is at depth 3, beyond `-maxdepth 2`.

options.t: Nothing, because the pattern `*.txt` does not match the names with a slash in them.
options.why: `-name` is compared with the last component of each path, so the pattern matches.

questions.title: The empty file
questions.text: `empty.txt` is a regular file with 0 bytes. Which statement about the four tests `[ -e empty.txt ]`, `[ -f empty.txt ]`, `[ -s empty.txt ]` and `[ -d empty.txt ]` is TRUE?

options.t: Only `-e` succeeds, because the file has no content at all.
options.why: `-f` succeeds too: it is a regular file.

options.t: `-e`, `-f` and `-s` succeed, and only `-d` fails.
options.why: `-s` needs the file to exist and have content; this one is empty.

options.t: `-e` and `-f` succeed, while `-s` and `-d` fail.
options.why: It exists and is a regular file, but it is not empty (`-s`) and not a directory (`-d`).

options.t: Only `-d` fails, since the file exists and is regular.
options.why: `-s` fails as well, since the file has no data.

questions.title: The redirection that eats an argument
questions.text: What is the difference between `ls | wc -l` and `ls > wc -l`?

options.t: Both of them count the entries of the directory, and the second one saves the result in a file.
options.why: The second command does not run `wc`.

options.t: The first counts the lines `ls` prints; the second runs `ls -l` and writes into a file named `wc`.
options.why: After `> wc` the word `-l` is an ordinary argument of `ls`.

options.t: The first one is correct and the second one is a syntax error, since `wc` is not a file.
options.why: It is valid syntax; it simply does something different.

options.t: The first sends the output of `ls` to `wc`; the second sends the output of `wc` to `ls`.
options.why: Neither of them sends output to `ls`.

questions.title: Forcing a password change
questions.text: Which command makes the user `ana` choose a new password the next time she logs in?

options.t: `passwd -l ana`
options.why: `-l` locks the account, so she could not log in with a password at all.

options.t: `passwd -u ana`
options.why: `-u` unlocks an account that was locked; it does not expire the password.

options.t: `passwd -e ana`
options.why: `-e` expires the password: it must be changed at the next login.

options.t: `deluser ana`
options.why: It removes the user instead of asking for a new password.

questions.title: Sorting inside top
questions.text: `top` shows the processes sorted by CPU use. Which key sorts them by memory use instead?

options.t: `M` (Shift+M)
options.why: It changes the sort column to memory use.
It opens the help screen with the list of options.
It quits `top`.
It asks for the PID of a process to send it a signal; it does not change the order.

questions.title: A whole word
questions.text: `w` contains the lines `cat`, `concat`, `catalog` and `the cat sat`. Which command prints only the lines that contain `cat` as a whole word?

options.t: `grep cat w`
options.why: It matches `cat` anywhere, so it prints all four lines.

options.t: `grep '\<cat' w`
options.why: It anchors only the beginning of the word, so `catalog` also matches.

options.t: `grep '^cat$' w`
options.why: It matches only a line that is exactly `cat`, and misses `the cat sat`.

options.t: `grep -w cat w`
options.why: `-w` requires the match to be a whole word, giving `cat` and `the cat sat`.

questions.title: Writing through a link to a directory
questions.text:
```
mkdir d; echo 1 > d/f
ln -s d link
echo 2 >> link/f
cat d/f
rm link
ls d
```
What does this print?

options.t: `1`, `2` and then nothing for `ls`, because `rm link` removed the directory.
options.why: `rm` on a symbolic link removes only the link.

options.t: `1` and `f`, because `link/f` is a different file.
options.why: `link/f` is `d/f`, reached through the link, so the line `2` is added to it.
The append goes through the link to `d/f`; removing the link leaves `d` and its file untouched.

options.t: `2` and `f`, because `>>` replaces the content.
options.why: `>>` appends, so `1` stays.

questions.title: Command substitution
questions.text: Which statement about command substitution is FALSE?

options.t: `n=$(ls | wc -l)` stores the number of entries in `n`.
options.why: True: the output of the command replaces `$( )`.

options.t: `echo "Hi $(whoami)"` is expanded even between double quotes.
options.why: True: double quotes allow substitutions.

options.t: Backticks, as in `` `date` ``, do the same as `$(date)`.
options.why: True: it is the older syntax for the same thing.

options.t: `echo '$(date)'` prints the current date.
options.why: False: single quotes prevent the substitution, so it prints the text `$(date)`.

questions.title: tee, paste and split
questions.text: Which statement about `tee`, `paste` and `split` is FALSE?

options.t: `ls | tee list.txt` shows the listing on the screen and also saves it in `list.txt`.
options.why: True: `tee` writes its input to the file and to stdout.

options.t: `split -l 2 f` cuts `f` into pieces of two lines each, named `xaa`, `xab`, and so on.
options.why: True.

options.t: `paste a b` joins line 1 of `a` with line 1 of `b`, separated by a tab, then the lines 2, and so on.
options.why: True: it pastes the files side by side.

options.t: `paste a b` prints all of `a` and then all of `b`.
options.why: False: that is what `cat a b` does.
